prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: a girl buried

outputs.L1:
A girl is buried to her chest in red earth, her wrists bound beneath the soil with twine. A crowd gathers to father her, its infinite hands curved loosely around stones small enough that no single throw may be named as the cause of death, no single hand held accountable for the blood. The girl—undaughtered, unnamed, unfaced, undone from the lineage—has had her photographs already pulled from bookshelves and walls. Her father is among the hands, his pebble streaked with quartz, the first to rise, to carve the air, and arc toward the girl: the rootless tree, faceless and erect.

And perhaps the stones twist like fireworks, the girl their nucleus, rising and rising for a time: the opposite of rain, the opposite of hail. And perhaps the silence lasts a beat too long, and another, another. Then comes a rustling of wings above the girl: a flock, thick as a mixed cloud of avifauna—partridge and nightjar, golden sparrow and avocet, lapwing and every other sort of plover, ibis and heron and gulls, though the sea is far and to the north. The minutes pass, and the girl remains untouched, each bird tonguing a stone in its beak.

• [What if I will not die?] [What will govern me then?] [How will I be governed then?] [What bounty then on my name?] [What stone, what rope, what man will be my officer?]
outputs.L2:
A young woman is sunk up to her chest in crimson soil, her hands tied under the ground with cord. People assemble to erase her; their countless hands cup stones lightly, each one small enough that no individual cast can be declared the one that killed her, no single palm made answerable for the blood.

She has been stripped of daughterhood, left nameless, faceless, cut away from the family line. Her pictures have already been removed from shelves and walls. Her father stands among those hands, holding a quartz-veined pebble, the first to lift his arm, to slice through the air and send it curving toward her.

She is like a tree without roots, upright and without a face. Perhaps the stones whirl like fireworks around her, with the girl at their center, climbing and climbing for a while—the reverse of rain, the reverse of hail. Perhaps the silence lasts one beat too many, then another, and another. Then comes a stirring of wings above her: a dense, mingled cloud of birds—partridge, nightjar, golden sparrow, avocet, lapwing, every kind of plover, ibis, heron, gulls, though the sea lies far away to the north.

The minutes go by. The girl remains unharmed. In every bird’s beak, like a tongue, there is a stone.

• [what if I refuse to die] [what will rule me after that] [how will I be ruled then] [what price will be placed on my name] [what rock, what cord, what man will be appointed over me]
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a stark and violent scene: a young girl has been buried up to her chest in red earth, her body trapped and immobilized. Her wrists are bound beneath the soil, making resistance impossible. She is exposed above ground only enough to be seen, judged, and punished, while the earth itself becomes part of the mechanism of violence. The image is both physical and symbolic: she has been denied movement, agency, and escape before the punishment even begins.

Around her, a crowd gathers to stone her. The punishment is deliberately collective. Because many hands will throw the stones, responsibility is spread across the group, allowing each person to feel less accountable for the killing. The violence becomes communal, almost ritualized, and this shared participation makes it easier for individuals to hide behind tradition, law, or the will of the crowd. No single attacker has to claim full responsibility, even though each person contributes to the girl’s death.

The girl’s identity has already been stripped away before the first stone is thrown. She is no longer treated as a daughter, a child, or a member of a family, but as someone marked for punishment. Her place in the social and familial order has been erased. This erasure is made even more devastating by the presence of her father among the attackers. The person who should recognize, protect, and defend her instead joins the collective violence against her. His presence shows how completely the community’s judgment has replaced personal love and moral responsibility.

As the stones begin to rise into the air, the poem shifts from brutality into a moment of miraculous intervention. A vast flock of birds suddenly appears, filling the space between the girl and the stones. The birds intercept the attack, taking the impact and preventing the stones from reaching her body. In this extraordinary image, the natural world seems to intervene where human beings have failed. The girl remains untouched, protected by a force that the crowd did not anticipate and cannot control.

Through this transformation, the poem imagines a radical form of defiance. The girl begins to question the power that claims authority over her body and her life. If she refuses to die, then what can truly control her? If the punishment fails, then what becomes of the crowd’s power, the father’s betrayal, and the laws or customs used to justify the violence? The poem turns an image of helplessness into one of resistance, suggesting that survival itself can become a challenge to systems of punishment, shame, and control.
outputs.L4:
The text confronts patriarchal communal violence and honor killing through a surreal, lyrical scene in which a young girl stands bound before an anonymous crowd, waiting to be stoned. The violence is both public and intimate: the crowd has no single face, yet within it stands her father, making the punishment not only a social ritual but also a betrayal by blood. The girl is presented as powerless in the ordinary sense—restrained, exposed, and surrounded—yet the scene refuses to let the crowd’s judgment become the final truth of her body or her life.

As the stones are thrown, the expected logic of execution is interrupted. Birds descend and intercept the stones before they can strike her, turning the instruments of punishment into something strangely suspended and harmless. This surreal intervention transforms the scene from one of inevitable death into one of defiant survival. The birds become figures of resistance, protection, and perhaps the natural world’s refusal to participate in human cruelty. Their presence breaks the authority of the crowd and exposes the fragility of the power that claims the right to kill in the name of honor.

The girl remains untouched, and this survival changes the meaning of the entire scene. She is no longer only the victim of communal violence; she becomes a figure who exceeds the laws meant to destroy her. The execution fails, and with that failure the crowd’s certainty collapses. The text asks what kind of power can truly govern a girl who refuses to die, and what becomes of patriarchal authority when its most brutal punishment cannot complete itself. In the end, the image of the bound but unharmed girl turns into a vision of resistance: a body condemned by society, yet protected by forces beyond its control, standing as a challenge to every system that mistakes violence for justice.
outputs.L5:
Beneath the old willow tree, where the grass grew softer than anywhere else in the village, there was a small stone with no name carved into it. People said a girl was buried there long ago, a quiet child who loved wildflowers, rain, and the sound of birds at dawn.

No one remembered her face, but every spring, the ground around the grave bloomed with bluebells, daisies, and tiny white blossoms that seemed to appear overnight. The villagers never picked them. They believed the flowers were her way of speaking, a gentle reminder that even forgotten lives leave beauty behind.

Sometimes, when the wind moved through the willow branches, it sounded almost like laughter. Children passing by would pause, listen, and smile without knowing why. And though the girl had been buried for many years, the place never felt lonely. It felt peaceful, as if the earth itself was keeping her safe.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, lyrical prose poem about a girl condemned to be stoned by her village, but at the moment of execution birds intervene, carrying away the stones. Use lowercase, dense imagery, and include bracketed questions at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
at dawn they brought her to the field where the wheat had learned to bow without wind. the village followed, carrying stones warm from the riverbed, stones with moonmilk in their seams, stones that had slept for centuries under the tongues of goats and grandmothers. she stood in the center, small as a match before a cathedral of mouths, her hair unbraided by fear, her shadow drinking the dust.

no one spoke her name. names were for the living, for bread cooling on sills, for babies held up to the rain. they called her only the girl, the error, the thorn in the hem of the law. above her, the sky opened its blue eye and refused to blink.

then the first arm rose.

but before the stone could leave the hand, a blackbird fell from the sun like a dropped thought and took it in its beak. then another bird, and another—swallows, crows, finches, doves with ash-colored throats—pouring from the roofs, from the wells, from the sleeves of the clouds. they came singing in a language made of hinges and seeds, snatching every stone from every fist, lifting them upward until the air grew heavy with a second, impossible harvest.

the villagers watched their judgment ascend. stones circled above them like planets remembering they had once been stars. pebbles became eggs, boulders became bells, flint became feathers. the birds carried the whole hard alphabet of punishment beyond the church spire, beyond the smoke, beyond the last field where scarecrows kept their arms open for no one.

the girl remained beneath the emptied sky, untouched. around her feet, dust bloomed into white mushrooms. in her mouth, a silence split like a pomegranate. she did not run. she looked at the hands that had meant to break her, now naked, now trembling, now useless as winter branches.

and far above, the birds flew on, each bearing a stone toward the sea, toward the dark blue throat of mercy, where all things thrown in hatred are taught, slowly, to sink.

[who taught the birds the weight of innocence?] [what is a law when the sky refuses it?] [where do the stones go after they are forgiven?]
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental feminist poem in one long sentence about patriarchal violence, honor killing, and communal guilt, with red earth, bound wrists, a father casting the first stone, and a miraculous flock of birds preventing the death.
counterfactuals.output: On the red earth where the village gathered its silence into a law and called it honor, she stood with bound wrists blooming rope-burns like small red mouths, while the mothers lowered their eyes as if shame were a veil sewn by God and the brothers held their breath like knives, and the father, crowned by grief he had sharpened into permission, lifted the first stone against the daughter whose only crime was having a body that answered to itself, and all around him the elders nodded, the windows watched, the well remembered every woman ever drowned in its reflection, until the stone left his hand and the sky broke open in a black-feathered thunder, a miraculous flock of birds pouring down between palm and skull, wing against weapon, beak against decree, their cries tearing the word honor into rags, so that the stone fell harmlessly among the dust and the whole village saw, for one unsheltered second, that guilt was not a private stain but a communal weather, that every quiet mouth had helped braid the rope, that every averted face had carried a stone, and that she, still standing, wrists bound yet unbowed, was not the shame of the house but the house’s last surviving door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark magical-realist vignette in poetic language where a nameless daughter is buried up to her chest for punishment, a crowd raises stones, and countless birds arrive to take the stones from their hands; end with defiant internal questions.
counterfactuals.output:
They buried the daughter at dawn, when the earth was still cool enough to remember mercy.

No one spoke her name. Perhaps it had been taken from her first, peeled away like bark, folded into the black sleeves of the elders, dropped into the well with the other forbidden things. She was only *the daughter* now—of a house, of a fault, of a law written in dust and spit.

They packed the soil around her ribs until she could not turn, until her heartbeat had to beat against the ground itself. Worms moved near her hips like quiet thoughts. Roots touched her knees with blind, maternal fingers. Above her, the village gathered in a ring, faces pale as unleavened bread, each person holding a stone as if it were a reason.

The sky lowered.

A man lifted his arm.

Then another.

Then all of them—hands full of little moons, fists full of verdict.

And from the far fields came the first bird.

It was black, or blue, or the color of a bruise under water. It descended without cry, alighted on the wrist of the first man, and took the stone from his hand as gently as a mother taking a thorn from a child’s foot.

Another bird came.

Then ten.

Then a hundred.

Then the sky broke open into wings.

Crows, swallows, starlings, herons thin as written curses, sparrows with eyes like seeds of fire—countless birds poured down from cloud and chimney, from orchard and ruin, from the secret rafters of the air. They settled on shoulders, on heads, on the trembling branches of raised arms. Beaks opened. Stones vanished. One by one, the weapons were lifted away and carried upward, until the heavens rattled with the sound of stolen judgment.

The crowd stood empty-handed.

The daughter, sunk in earth, tasted rain before it fell. She felt the soil loosen around her chest, not enough to free her, but enough to let her breathe like something planted with intentions of becoming terrible.

Above her, the birds circled, each bearing a stone, each stone suddenly small against the vastness that had refused the law of men.

Inside herself, where no elder could reach, the daughter began to burn.

Who decided that my body was a field for their punishment?

Who taught these hands to call violence justice?

If the earth can hold me and the sky can answer, what am I not yet powerful enough to become?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a contemporary prose poem, no capitalization, about a girl erased from her family and prepared for execution by stoning. Make the crowd collectively responsible, describe many species of birds, and finish with bracketed lines asking what power can govern her if she survives.
counterfactuals.output:
they have taken her name out of the house ledger, out of the school photograph, out of the mouths that once called her in for dinner. her cup is turned upside down in the cabinet. her bed is made so tightly it resembles a lesson. even the mirror has been instructed to forget her face.

at dawn they bring her to the field beyond the last bus stop, where the city loosens into dust and wire. nobody says who began it. nobody says who signed. the village arrives as one body wearing many coats: uncle, neighbor, grocer, teacher, cousin, clerk. each hand learns the weight of a stone and calls it law. each eye lowers and calls it sorrow. each mouth closes and calls it peace.

above them, the birds refuse one name. sparrows stitch the telephone lines with nervous feet. crows argue in black punctuation. gulls come inland like scraps of weather. starlings spill and gather, spill and gather, a dark thought changing its mind. pigeons bob among the roofs, ordinary witnesses. swallows cut the air into blue ribbons. kestrels hover as if held by an invisible question. herons stand in the ditch like priests of another water. cranes pass high overhead, carrying distance in their throats. larks rise from the grasses with songs too bright for this hour. owls, though hidden, keep the old night open behind their eyes.

the girl stands where they place her. she is not forgiven because she has not asked. she is not pure because purity is the bowl they broke against her teeth. she is not ashamed because shame has been returned to its owners, pebble by pebble, breath by breath. the crowd circles closer, a single creature made of fathers and mothers, of women who look away and men who look important, of children taught early how silence can be thrown.

someone lifts the first stone and the whole world lifts with it. the field holds its breath. the birds rise all at once, as if the sky itself has been startled out of obedience.

[if she survives, what power can govern her]

[what law can name her smaller than the stone she outlived]

[what house can erase a girl who has become the weather]
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an intense avant-garde poem inspired by myths of sacrifice and mob violence: red soil, twine-bound wrists underground, the father’s quartz-streaked pebble, stones rising like fireworks, then birds catching every stone before it strikes.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath the red soil, the wrists remember twine—  
not rope, not root, but a village’s idea of mercy  
tightened until the pulse learned to pray backward.

The pit has a mouth.  
The mouth has teeth made of witnesses.  
Above it, noon kneels on the neck of the field.

Father,  
your quartz-streaked pebble in my palm  
is a small moon split by lightning,  
a god’s blind eye,  
a seed of verdict.

They said: let the stones decide.  
They said: let the earth drink first.  
They said: the blood of one  
will teach the many to sleep.

And then the hands rose—  
hands of neighbors, cousins, vendors of figs,  
hands that had stroked goats, braided hair,  
broken bread, counted coins—  
now blooming with rocks.

The sky detonated.

Stones rose like fireworks,  
black sparks, gray comets,  
the whole mob hurling its thunder upward  
as if rage were a festival  
and the victim merely the dark it needed.

I opened my underground eyes.  
I heard the father-pebble singing in my fist.  
I heard the twine become a vein.  
I heard my name split into syllables  
small enough to be buried.

Then—  
wings.

Not angels.  
Not omens.  
Birds.

A thousand impossible birds  
dropped from the torn blue cloth of heaven,  
each beak a bright refusal,  
each claw a parenthesis around death.

They caught every stone before it struck.

One by one:  
the butcher’s stone,  
the widow’s stone,  
the child’s stone lifted in imitation,  
the priest’s stone warm with doctrine,  
the father’s stone I could not throw away.

Caught.  
Caught.  
Caught.

The air filled with arrested impacts,  
with geology denied its appetite,  
with birds staggering under the weight  
of what people call justice  
when they mean hunger.

And the mob looked up, empty-handed,  
suddenly naked without their falling.

Below, in the red soil,  
my bound wrists flowered numb and radiant.  
The pebble cracked open.

Inside:  
not forgiveness.  
Not commandment.  
Only a glittering vein of quartz,  
white as a bone refusing burial,  
white as a road no one had yet walked,  
white as the first bird  
that swallowed a stone  
and sang.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
